procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court in Bombay, given the High Court's appellate jurisdiction.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 18, 1962 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1426 of 1968 and confirmation Case No. 21 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court dismissed the appeal of Moti alias Narayan Shesharina Yadav (accused No. 2) and confirmed the conviction of Sheshanna Bhumanna Yadav (accused No. 3). However, the High Court altered the conviction of accused No. 2 from murder under section 302 to an offence under section 302 read with section 120B and section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed the death sentence for accused No. 3 but reduced the punishment of accused No. 2 (who was 17 years old) to rigorous imprisonment for life.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appeal to the Supreme Court was made by special leave. The appellant is not explicitly named, but it is implied to be one or both of the accused, likely challenging the High Court's judgment.

directions: The accused will surrender to his bail, if any.

issue.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the crime.

facts: A father and son (accused No. 3 and No. 2) were convicted of murdering a 15-year-old boy and committing theft from his grandfather's house.
The main evidence against them was the testimony of an approver (an accomplice named Dinkar).
The High Court had previously found that there was sufficient corroboration connecting both accused to the murder and theft.
The appellant argued in the Supreme Court that there was no corroboration of actual participation in the murder.
law: The Court relied on sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act, which state that while an accomplice is a competent witness, it is a rule of caution that it is unsafe to convict on their testimony alone without corroboration.

Citing prior cases (Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab and Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab), the Court outlined a three-part test for approver evidence: 1) the approver must be a reliable witness, 2) there must be reliable corroboration, and 3) the corroboration must be sufficient in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime.
Corroboration is defined as confirmatory evidence, which can come from another witness or from circumstances, such as the conduct of the accused.
The corroborating evidence must confirm the part of the testimony that suggests the crime was committed by the accused, not just any part of the story.
application: The Court first determined that the approver, Dinkar, was a reliable witness.

The Court then identified numerous pieces of corroborating evidence for both accused, including: their joint sale of a stolen cycle carrier, the son's production of stolen cloth, the father's sale of other stolen items, and the son's suspicious behavior in retrieving a stolen cloth from a tailor.
The Court noted the close relationship between the accused (father and son) and their close association in disposing of the stolen articles.

It reasoned that the murder and theft were part of the same transaction due to their close proximity in time. Therefore, evidence corroborating the theft also served to corroborate their involvement in the entire criminal act, including the murder.
The Court found that all the pieces of evidence, taken together, provided sufficient corroboration of the approver's testimony in material particulars.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was sufficient corroboration of the approver's evidence in material particulars. The evidence connected both accused not only with the theft but also with the murder, as they were part of a single transaction. Therefore, the Court accepted that the legal requirement for corroboration was met.

issue.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to accused No. 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence.

facts.fact: Corroborating evidence against Accused No. 2 (the son) included: his statement leading to the discovery of stolen articles; being seen with the approver and a boy matching the victim's description on the day of the crime; producing a piece of cloth identical to one from the victim's home; pledging the victim's cycle; and selling other stolen items like utensils and a cycle carrier.

Corroborating evidence against Accused No. 3 (the father) included: a motive, as he was in legal disputes with the victim's grandfather over a house; his name being found in a witness's notebook; giving stolen silver articles to a witness (Takalkar) to sell and store; and joining his son (Accused No. 2) in selling the stolen cycle carrier.
The court noted the close relationship (father and son) and their joint actions in disposing of the stolen property shortly after the crime.

law.law_text: Corroboration is confirmatory evidence from another witness or from circumstances, such as the conduct of the accused.
Corroborative evidence must implicate the accused in material particulars, meaning it must confirm the part of the testimony suggesting the crime was committed by the accused.

application.application_text: The Court determined that the murder and the theft were not separate events but a single, 'composite' transaction.

Based on this, the evidence that corroborated the accuseds' involvement in the theft (such as their possession and sale of the stolen articles) also served as sufficient corroboration for their involvement in the murder, as described by the approver.

The Court found that the numerous pieces of evidence, including witness sightings, the discovery of stolen goods linked to both accused, and their joint actions, directly connected both Accused No. 2 and No. 3 to the crime in material particulars.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that there was sufficient corroboration of the approver's evidence in material particulars to prove that both Accused No. 2 and Accused No. 3 were guilty of the offence.

issue.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the approver's story about the conspiracy and the common intention by way of a pre-conceived plan to murder Narendra.

facts.fact: The murder and the subsequent theft of items from the victim's house were considered to be a single, 'composite unit' or transaction.
Accused No. 3 had a motive to commit the crime, stemming from civil and criminal disputes with the victim's grandfather, Dr. Nanavati, over a bungalow.
Accused No. 3 proposed the murder to the approver, Dinkar, and suggested that his own son, Accused No. 2, should also be involved.
Accused No. 3 was directly linked to the disposal of the stolen property. He gave silver articles to a witness, Takalkar, to sell, and these items were later recovered by the police and identified.
Witnesses saw the victim, Narendra, alive in the company of Accused No. 2 and the approver shortly before the murder.
The approver led police to the place where the victim's remains (skull, bone, hair) and belongings (a shirt and chain, identified by family) were discovered.

law.law: To rely on an approver's testimony, the court must first be satisfied that the approver is a reliable witness.
Once reliability is established, the approver's evidence requires corroboration in material particulars that connect the accused with the crime.

application.application: The Court first determined that the approver, Dinkar, was a reliable witness.

The Court then linked the murder and the theft as parts of the same transaction. It reasoned that since the events were a 'composite unit,' evidence corroborating the accused's involvement in the theft also served to corroborate their involvement in the entire conspiracy, including the murder.

The evidence of Accused No. 3 disposing of the stolen goods, the close association between the accused, and the proximity in time between the murder and theft were all seen as material particulars that corroborated the approver's story of a pre-conceived plan.
The testimony of independent witnesses placing the victim with the accused, and the discovery of the victim's remains based on the approver's information, further strengthened the approver's account.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the High Court's conclusion that there was sufficient corroboration of the approver's evidence. The key to this decision was treating the murder and theft as a single transaction, which allowed evidence related to the theft to corroborate the approver's testimony about the entire conspiracy and the common intention to murder.

arguments.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the crime.
appellant_arguments: There was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder.
The evidence might support a charge of theft, but not murder.
respondent_arguments: There was sufficient corroboration connecting the accused not only with the offence of theft but also with the murder.
Evidence such as the pre-existing civil and criminal proceedings between accused No. 3 and the deceased's grandfather established a motive for the crime.
The testimony of the washerman, who saw accused No. 2 and the approver with a boy matching the deceased's description, corroborates the crime.

arguments.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to accused No. 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence.
appellant_arguments: There was no corroboration of actual participation in the murder.
Accused No. 3 could be guilty of theft but not of murder.
respondent_arguments: For accused No. 3 (the father), corroborating evidence included: pre-existing disputes with the deceased's family, selling articles belonging to the deceased's grandfather, providing a piece of cloth linked to the crime, and joining his son in selling a cycle carrier.

For accused No. 2 (the son), corroborating evidence included: the discovery of articles in a godown as a result of his statement, the washerman's testimony placing him with the deceased, and going with his father to sell the cycle carrier.
The relationship of father and son between the accused is also a relevant factor.

arguments.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the approver's story about the conspiracy and the common intention by way of a pre-conceived plan to murder Narendra.
appellant_arguments: There was no corroboration of a pre-conceived plan or common intention to murder, as the evidence did not sufficiently prove participation in the murder itself.
respondent_arguments: The evidence of the approver regarding the conspiracy and common intention was corroborated in material particulars.
The joint actions of the accused, such as selling the cycle carrier together, and the evidence establishing motive, supported the existence of a pre-conceived plan.

cases.case_name: Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the corroboration of accomplice evidence, the court must be satisfied that: (1) the accomplice is a reliable witness; (2) there is reliable corroboration of the accomplice's evidence; and (3) there is sufficient corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime.

cases.case_name: Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the corroboration of accomplice evidence, the court must be satisfied that: (1) the accomplice is a reliable witness; (2) there is reliable corroboration of the accomplice's evidence; and (3) there is sufficient corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where multiple offenses, such as murder and theft, are committed in close proximity of time and form part of the same composite transaction, evidence that provides sufficient corroboration for an approver's testimony regarding parts of the transaction can serve as sufficient corroboration for the approver's entire testimony concerning the whole transaction, provided the approver is found to be a reliable witness.
obiter: If a witness testifies that an accused stole sheep and hid the skins in a certain place, the discovery of the skins in that place does not, by itself, corroborate the evidence against the accused. However, if the skins were found in the accused's house, this would be corroborative as it tends to confirm the accused had a role in the theft.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the murder and the subsequent theft were not separate events but formed a single, composite transaction. Because the murder and theft were inextricably linked by their close proximity in time and the shared motive, the substantial evidence corroborating the approver's testimony regarding the theft—such as the accused's joint disposal of stolen property and the discovery of articles based on their statements—also served as sufficient corroboration in material particulars for the approver's testimony about the murder and the underlying conspiracy.
legal_tests_applied: The law of corroboration of accomplice evidence, which requires that an approver's testimony be corroborated in material particulars, as established in precedents like Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab and Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the evidence only supported a charge of theft and not murder by holding that the two crimes were part of the same transaction. The court found, 'The close proximity of time between the murder and theft points to the inescapable conclusion that they formed part of the same transaction.'

The appellant's claim of a lack of corroboration for the murder itself was defeated because the court ruled that evidence connecting the accused to the theft also connected them to the murder, as the 'transaction was one composite unit of murdering Narendra and committing theft.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the murder and theft were a 'composite unit,' meaning evidence corroborating one part of the transaction corroborated the whole, including the murder.

The court found sufficient corroboration in material particulars against both accused, citing specific evidence: the motive of accused No. 3 arising from disputes with the deceased's grandfather, the discovery of stolen articles in a godown as a result of a statement by accused No. 2, the joint action where 'Accused No. 2 and 3 went together for the sale of cycle carrier,' and the fact that the 'relationship of father and son between accused No. 3 and accused No. 2 is not to be lost sight of.'
policy_considerations: The court applied a heightened standard of review due to the severity of the punishment, stating, 'In view of the fact that there was capital sentence of accused No. 3 we went through the evidence to find out as to whether there was any infirmity in evidence. We have found none.'
